title: Care is organized through multigenerational living, unpaid substitution, and gendered work tradeoffs
source_unit: Federal Reserve Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking adult respondent, 2025; living-arrangement, childcare, and adult-care tables

denominator.unit: published percentage base among all adults

under_30_lives_with_parent.unit: percent of adults under age 30; 6 percentage points above 2022 and 12 above 2019

age_60_plus_lives_alone.unit: percent of adults age 60 or older

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published living-arrangement estimates; respondents could select multiple household relationships.
observations.uncertainty: Cross-sectional household composition does not identify whether co-residence is chosen, affordable, protective, crowded, or driven by care need; household and person units are not interchangeable.
observations.subgroup: All adults, adults under age 30, and adults age 60 or older.
observations.counterinterpretation: Multigenerational living can provide care, housing, income pooling, and belonging rather than indicate constraint; living alone can reflect preference as well as unmet support.

observations.period: 2025 SHED; paid childcare and housing-cost comparison

denominator.unit: published conditional bases among adults living with their own children under age 13; expense comparison conditions on positive payments

any_paid_childcare_under_13.unit: percent of parents of young children using paid childcare in the prior week

any_paid_childcare_income_under_50k.unit: percent of parents of children under 13 with family income below $50,000

any_paid_childcare_income_100k_plus.unit: percent of parents of children under 13 with family income of $100,000 or more

median_monthly_childcare_payment.unit: US dollars among families paying for childcare and housing

median_monthly_housing_payment_comparato.unit: US dollars among families paying for childcare and housing

childcare_to_housing_median_ratio.unit: ratio of median monthly childcare to median monthly housing payment

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published childcare-use and expense estimates; childcare and housing payment medians use the report's separate positive-payment universes.
observations.uncertainty: The weekly childcare measure and monthly payment comparison are different reference periods and conditional populations; the source does not identify quality, availability, commute, work schedule, or unpaid alternatives for each family.
observations.subgroup: Parents living with their own children under age 13, conditioned by family income and positive childcare/housing payments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher paid-care use among higher-income families may reflect greater employment, desired care, or affordability rather than greater need; lower paid-care use can mean unpaid support, nonemployment, unavailable care, or unaffordability.

observations.period: 2025 SHED; unpaid childcare by family/employment structure

denominator.unit: published conditional bases among adults living with their own children under age 13

any_unpaid_childcare.unit: percent of parents of children under age 13

paid_childcare_one_working_parent.unit: percent of households with one working and one non-working parent

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published paid/unpaid childcare estimates by family and employment structure; paid and unpaid categories are separate responses.
observations.uncertainty: The data do not identify hours, provider reliability, schedule control, work quality, or whether unpaid care displaced rest, paid work, education, or another household activity; categories may coexist.
observations.subgroup: Parents living with their own children under age 13, grouped by partnership and employment structure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Unpaid care can be a preferred or supportive arrangement; more use among working single parents may reflect network strength, necessity, or both.

observations.period: 2025 SHED; gendered childcare and adult-care work effects

denominator.unit: published conditional bases among parents of children under age 13, non-working parents, and adults providing unpaid adult care

mothers_primary_caretaker_with_partner_a.unit: percent of mothers versus 12% of fathers in the same living-arrangement frame

working_mothers_primary_caretaker_dual_e.unit: percent of working mothers versus 8% of working fathers

mothers_not_working_parents_under_13.unit: percent of mothers versus 18% of fathers among parents living with children under 13

adult_care_any.unit: percent of adults regularly providing unpaid care to an adult relative or friend

prime_age_adult_carers_without_paid_job.unit: percent of prime-age adults caring for another adult versus 23% without that responsibility

daily_prime_age_carers_without_paid_job.unit: percent of prime-age adults providing daily adult care

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2025 SHED published caretaker, employment, and adult-care estimates; caretaker identity and employment measures use separate conditional universes.
observations.uncertainty: The survey is cross-sectional and self-reported; caretaker roles can reflect preference, norms, income, schedule, household composition, or care intensity. Adult-care questions exclude irregular or very low-frequency care by design.
observations.subgroup: Parents of children under age 13, mothers/fathers, working parents, non-working parents, and prime-age adult caregivers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Caregiving can provide meaning, reciprocity, and family support; association with nonemployment does not establish that care caused a work exit or that paid work would be preferable.

related_sources.claim: ATUS supplies diary-day time allocation and care-work measurement with a different unit and design.
related_sources.access_boundary: Annual SHED care and employment responses are not diary minutes or the same respondents.

related_sources.claim: The 2025 SHED income-and-expenses chapter supplies budget-margin and outside-support context for care costs.
related_sources.access_boundary: Care spending and household financial support are separate response surfaces.

boundary: This record establishes 2025 population-level living arrangements, paid and unpaid childcare, adult caregiving, gendered caretaker roles, and caregiving/employment associations. It does not establish a causal childcare-price or caregiving effect, care quality, schedule control, household recovery, trust, political action, or a same-family longitudinal displacement path. Paid care, unpaid care, co-residence, nonemployment, and meaning remain separate stages.
